notes.front: On GitHub, what is a personal account?
notes.back: The kind of user account you are using if you signed up for your own account on GitHub.com.
notes.explanation: Each personal account uses either the GitHub Free or the GitHub Pro plan.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Types of GitHub accounts”, “Personal accounts”
notes.evidence: If you signed up for your own account on GitHub.com, you are using a personal account. Each personal account uses either GitHub Free or GitHub Pro.
notes.example: A student who signs up on GitHub.com to keep her coursework has a personal account.

notes.front: On GitHub, what is a managed user account?
notes.back: A user account created for you by an enterprise on GitHub Enterprise Cloud.
notes.explanation: Some of its details and settings are managed by the enterprise that created it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Types of GitHub accounts”, “Managed user accounts”
notes.evidence: If your account was created for you by an enterprise on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, you are using a managed user account. As a managed user account: * Some of your account details and settings are managed by your enterprise.
notes.example: Like a work email address your employer sets up and controls, rather than one you created yourself.

notes.front: On GitHub, what is an organization?
notes.back: A shared account where a large number of people can collaborate across many projects at once.
notes.explanation: Like user accounts, organizations can own resources such as repositories, packages and projects.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Types of GitHub accounts”, “Organization accounts”
notes.evidence: Organizations are shared accounts where a large number of people can collaborate across many projects at once. Like user accounts, organizations can own resources such as repositories, packages, and projects.
notes.example: A charity's volunteer developers share one organization that owns all the charity's repositories.

notes.front: On GitHub, what is an enterprise account?
notes.back: An account that lets administrators centrally manage policy and billing for multiple organizations.
notes.explanation: Enterprise accounts come with GitHub Enterprise Cloud and GitHub Enterprise Server, and they also enable innersourcing between the organizations.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Types of GitHub accounts”, “Enterprise accounts”
notes.evidence: GitHub Enterprise Cloud and GitHub Enterprise Server include enterprise accounts, which allow administrators to centrally manage policy and billing for multiple organizations and enable innersourcing between the organizations.
notes.example: A bank with separate organizations for retail, trading and technology sets their shared policies once, in one enterprise account.

notes.front: What does GitHub Free for personal accounts let you do with repositories?
notes.back: Work with unlimited collaborators on unlimited public repositories with a full feature set, and on unlimited private ones with a limited feature set.
notes.explanation: GitHub Free is one of the two plans a personal account can use; GitHub Pro is the other.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub's plans”, “GitHub Free for personal accounts”
notes.evidence: With GitHub Free for personal accounts, you can work with unlimited collaborators on unlimited public repositories with a full feature set, and on unlimited private repositories with a limited feature set.
notes.example: A hobbyist publishes an open source game on GitHub Free and has every feature on that public repository.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: What is GitHub Pro?
notes.back: A paid plan for personal accounts that adds features to GitHub Free, such as GitHub Support via email.
notes.explanation: Its additions include more GitHub Actions minutes and advanced tools and insights in private repositories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub's plans”, “GitHub Pro”
notes.evidence: In addition to the features available with GitHub Free for personal accounts, GitHub Pro includes: * GitHub Support via email * 3,000 GitHub Actions minutes per month
notes.example: A freelance developer with private client repositories upgrades her own account from Free to Pro.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: What is GitHub Team?
notes.back: A plan for organizations that adds to GitHub Free for organizations, including GitHub Support via email.
notes.explanation: Its additions include 3,000 GitHub Actions minutes per month and more GitHub Packages storage, among others.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub's plans”, “GitHub Team”
notes.evidence: In addition to the features available with GitHub Free for organizations, GitHub Team includes: * GitHub Support via email * 3,000 GitHub Actions minutes per month * 2 GB GitHub Packages storage
notes.example: A ten-person agency pays for GitHub Team on its organization so it can get support by email.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: What is GitHub Enterprise?
notes.back: A plan that adds to GitHub Team and comes as GitHub Enterprise Cloud or GitHub Enterprise Server.
notes.explanation: Its additions include GitHub Enterprise Support, single sign-on authentication and additional security, compliance and deployment controls.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub's plans”, “GitHub Enterprise”
notes.evidence: In addition to the features available with GitHub Team, GitHub Enterprise includes: * GitHub Enterprise Support * Additional security, compliance, and deployment controls * Authentication with SAML single sign-on
notes.example: A multinational that needs single sign-on for all staff chooses GitHub Enterprise.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: What is GitHub flow?
notes.back: A lightweight, branch-based workflow.
notes.explanation: The docs say it is useful for everyone, not just developers.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Introduction”
notes.evidence: GitHub flow is a lightweight, branch-based workflow. The GitHub flow is useful for everyone, not just developers.
notes.example: A team writing a policy document uses GitHub flow: each change is drafted on its own branch, reviewed, then merged.

notes.front: On GitHub, what is Markdown used for?
notes.back: Formatting your prose and code on GitHub with simple syntax.
notes.explanation: The same syntax works in comment fields and in .md files.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”
notes.evidence: Create sophisticated formatting for your prose and code on GitHub with simple syntax.
notes.example: Typing **done** in a comment so that the word shows in bold.

notes.front: In GitHub Markdown, what is a task list?
notes.back: A list whose items start with a hyphen, a space and [ ]; [x] marks a task as complete.
notes.explanation: The docs give this as the syntax for creating a task list.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Task lists”
notes.evidence: To create a task list, preface list items with a hyphen and space followed by `[ ]`. To mark a task as complete, use `[x]`.
notes.example: A checklist of three release chores in a comment, with the first one ticked.

notes.front: On GitHub, what is an @mention?
notes.back: Typing @ plus a person's username or a team name, which notifies them and brings their attention to the conversation.
notes.explanation: People are also notified if you edit a comment to add their username or team name.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Mentioning people and teams”
notes.evidence: This will trigger a notification and bring their attention to the conversation. People will also receive a notification if you edit a comment to mention their username or team name.
notes.example: Writing @sam in a comment so Sam is notified that the question is for him.

notes.front: In GitHub Markdown, what is an alert?
notes.back: A Markdown extension based on blockquote syntax, used to emphasise critical information.
notes.explanation: Alerts are also known as callouts or admonitions, and GitHub shows them with distinctive colours and icons.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Alerts”
notes.evidence: **Alerts**, also sometimes known as **callouts** or **admonitions**, are a Markdown extension based on the blockquote syntax that you can use to emphasize critical information.
notes.example: A coloured box at the top of a project's front page that warns readers not to run a script on a live server.

notes.front: What is GitHub Desktop?
notes.back: A free, open source application that helps you work with files hosted on GitHub or other Git hosting services.
notes.explanation: It has a graphical user interface that simplifies commands and helps you visualise changes.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Desktop”, “About GitHub Desktop”
notes.evidence: GitHub Desktop is a free, open source application that helps you to work with files hosted on GitHub or other Git hosting services.
notes.example: A designer commits changes to a website by clicking buttons in a window, never opening a terminal.

notes.front: What is GitHub Mobile?
notes.back: GitHub's app for Android and iOS, for doing high-impact work on GitHub quickly and from anywhere.
notes.explanation: The docs describe it as a safe and secure way to access your data through a trusted, first-party client application.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Mobile”, “About GitHub Mobile”
notes.evidence: GitHub Mobile is available as an Android and iOS app. GitHub Mobile gives you a way to do high-impact work on GitHub quickly and from anywhere.
notes.example: A maintainer clears her GitHub notifications on her phone while waiting for a train.

notes.front: Of GitHub's three types of account, which one does every person who uses GitHub sign in to?
notes.back: A user account.
notes.explanation: Your user account is your identity on GitHub, with a username and profile.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Types of GitHub accounts”, “About accounts”
notes.evidence: Every person who uses GitHub signs in to a user account.

notes.front: Of GitHub's three types of account, which one enhances collaboration between multiple users?
notes.back: An organization account.
notes.explanation: Organizations are shared accounts for many people collaborating across many projects.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Types of GitHub accounts”, “About accounts”
notes.evidence: An organization account enhances collaboration between multiple users

notes.front: Of GitHub's three types of account, which one allows central management of multiple organizations?
notes.back: An enterprise account.
notes.explanation: It sits above organizations, managing several of them from one place.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Types of GitHub accounts”, “About accounts”
notes.evidence: an enterprise account allows central management of multiple organizations.

notes.front: Any time you take an action on GitHub, such as creating an issue or reviewing a pull request, the action is attributed to your {{c1::user account}}.
notes.back: user account
notes.explanation: The docs describe your user account as your identity on GitHub.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Types of GitHub accounts”, “User accounts”
notes.evidence: Any time you take any action on GitHub, such as creating an issue or reviewing a pull request, the action is attributed to your user account.

notes.front: Can you sign in to an organization on GitHub?
notes.back: No. Each person signs in to their own user account, and actions on organization resources are attributed to that user account.
notes.explanation: An organization is a shared account that owns resources; people work in it through their own user accounts.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Types of GitHub accounts”, “Organization accounts”
notes.evidence: However, you cannot sign in to an organization. Instead, each person signs in to their user account, and any actions the person takes on organization resources are attributed to their user account.

notes.front: How many public and private repositories can a personal account own, and with how many collaborators?
notes.back: An unlimited number of each, with an unlimited number of collaborators.
notes.explanation: This holds for all personal accounts, whichever plan they use.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Types of GitHub accounts”, “Personal accounts”
notes.evidence: All personal accounts can own an unlimited number of public and private repositories, with an unlimited number of collaborators on those repositories.

notes.front: With a managed user account, what can you not do?
notes.back: Create public content or contribute to repositories outside the enterprise.
notes.explanation: You can still create your own private repositories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Types of GitHub accounts”, “Managed user accounts”
notes.evidence: You can create your own private repositories, but you cannot create public content or contribute to repositories outside the enterprise.

notes.front: How many organizations may an enterprise account contain?
notes.back: One or more.
notes.explanation: Organizations hold the places where non-admins typically work, such as repositories, discussions and projects.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Enterprise accounts”, “Organizations”
notes.evidence: An enterprise account may contain one or more organizations. Like an enterprise account, an organization account contains its own administrative features such as audit logs, policies, and teams. An organization also contains the places where non-admins typically do their work, such as repositories, discussions, and projects.

notes.front: A 12-person start-up wants its repositories owned by the company rather than by any one employee, with everyone signing in as themselves. Which account type fits?
notes.back: B: an organization.
notes.explanation: Organizations are shared accounts that can own repositories, while each person signs in to their own user account.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Types of GitHub accounts”, “Organization accounts”
notes.evidence: Organizations are shared accounts where a large number of people can collaborate across many projects at once. Like user accounts, organizations can own resources such as repositories, packages, and projects.
notes.choices:
A) One shared personal account
B) An organization
C) An enterprise account with no organizations
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: every person signs in to their own user account. C is wrong: an enterprise account exists to centrally manage multiple organizations.

notes.front: A university runs separate GitHub organizations for each faculty and wants to set policy and billing for all of them in one place. What does it need?
notes.back: A: an enterprise account.
notes.explanation: Enterprise accounts let administrators centrally manage policy and billing for multiple organizations.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Types of GitHub accounts”, “Enterprise accounts”
notes.evidence: enterprise accounts, which allow administrators to centrally manage policy and billing for multiple organizations
notes.choices:
A) An enterprise account
B) One more organization
C) A personal account for the head of technology
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: another organization would sit beside the others, not manage them. C is wrong: a personal account belongs to one person and does not manage organizations.

notes.front: Kofi's GitHub account was created for him by his employer's enterprise on GitHub Enterprise Cloud. He tries to open a public repository for a hobby project. What happens?
notes.back: A: he cannot; a managed user account cannot create public content.
notes.explanation: Managed user accounts can create their own private repositories but cannot create public content or contribute outside the enterprise.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Types of GitHub accounts”, “Managed user accounts”
notes.evidence: You can create your own private repositories, but you cannot create public content or contribute to repositories outside the enterprise.
notes.choices:
A) He cannot: managed user accounts cannot create public content
B) He can, like any personal account
C) He can, once he upgrades to GitHub Pro
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: his account was created by an enterprise, so it is a managed user account, not a personal account. C is wrong: GitHub Pro is a plan for personal accounts.

notes.front: Is GitHub Pro a type of account?
notes.back: No. It is a plan; a personal account uses either GitHub Free or GitHub Pro.
notes.explanation: Account types are user, organization and enterprise; plans such as Free and Pro sit on top of them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Types of GitHub accounts”, “Personal accounts”
notes.evidence: Each personal account uses either GitHub Free or GitHub Pro.

notes.front: If you use GitHub Free, what kind of feature set do private repositories owned by your personal account have, and how do you get the full set?
notes.back: A limited feature set; upgrade to GitHub Pro for the full set on private repositories.
notes.explanation: Public repositories get the full feature set on GitHub Free.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Types of GitHub accounts”, “Personal accounts”
notes.evidence: If you use GitHub Free, private repositories owned by your personal account have a limited feature set. You can upgrade to GitHub Pro to get a full feature set for private repositories.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: In GitHub Pro, what are two of the advanced tools added for private repositories?
notes.back: Two of: required pull request reviewers, protected branches, code owners (among others).
notes.explanation: GitHub Pro lists these under advanced tools and insights in private repositories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub's plans”, “GitHub Pro”
notes.evidence: Advanced tools and insights in private repositories: * Required pull request reviewers * Multiple pull request reviewers * Protected branches * Code owners
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: Mei works alone on private client repositories under her own personal account on GitHub Free and wants the full feature set on them. What should she do?
notes.back: A: upgrade her personal account to GitHub Pro.
notes.explanation: On GitHub Free, private repositories of a personal account have a limited feature set; GitHub Pro gives the full feature set.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Types of GitHub accounts”, “Personal accounts”
notes.evidence: You can upgrade to GitHub Pro to get a full feature set for private repositories.
notes.choices:
A) Upgrade to GitHub Pro
B) Buy GitHub Team for her personal account
C) Make the client repositories public
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: GitHub Team is a plan for organizations, not personal accounts. C is wrong: it would expose her clients' code rather than add features to private repositories.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: What are GitHub Enterprise's two deployment options, and how do they differ?
notes.back: GitHub Enterprise Cloud, hosted by GitHub in the cloud, and GitHub Enterprise Server, which is self-hosted.
notes.explanation: The two options differ in who hosts the service.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub's plans”, “GitHub Enterprise”
notes.evidence: GitHub Enterprise includes two deployment options: GitHub Enterprise Cloud, which is hosted by GitHub in the cloud, and GitHub Enterprise Server, which is self-hosted.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: A defence contractor must run GitHub on its own servers. Which option fits?
notes.back: C: GitHub Enterprise Server.
notes.explanation: GitHub Enterprise Server is the self-hosted deployment option of GitHub Enterprise.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub's plans”, “GitHub Enterprise”
notes.evidence: GitHub Enterprise Server, which is self-hosted.
notes.choices:
A) GitHub Team
B) GitHub Enterprise Cloud
C) GitHub Enterprise Server
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: Enterprise Cloud is hosted by GitHub in the cloud. A is wrong: GitHub Team is not one of GitHub Enterprise's deployment options.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: What is the first step of GitHub flow?
notes.back: Create a branch in your repository.
notes.explanation: Creating a branch gives you a space to work without affecting the default branch.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Create a branch”
notes.evidence: Create a branch in your repository.

notes.front: In GitHub flow, what step comes right after creating a branch?
notes.back: Make changes on your branch.
notes.explanation: The docs call your branch a safe place to make changes.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Make changes”
notes.evidence: On your branch, make any desired changes to the repository.

notes.front: In GitHub flow, what step comes right after making changes on your branch?
notes.back: Create a pull request.
notes.explanation: A pull request asks collaborators for feedback on your changes.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Create a pull request”
notes.evidence: Create a pull request to ask collaborators for feedback on your changes.

notes.front: In GitHub flow, what step comes right after creating a pull request?
notes.back: Address review comments.
notes.explanation: You can keep committing and pushing in response to reviews, and the pull request updates automatically.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Address review comments”
notes.evidence: You can continue to commit and push changes in response to the reviews. Your pull request will update automatically.

notes.front: In GitHub flow, what step comes once your pull request is approved?
notes.back: Merge your pull request.
notes.explanation: Merging makes your changes appear on the default branch.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Merge your pull request”
notes.evidence: Once your pull request is approved, merge your pull request. This will automatically merge your branch so that your changes appear on the default branch.

notes.front: What is the last step of GitHub flow, after you merge your pull request?
notes.back: Delete your branch.
notes.explanation: Deleting it indicates the work on the branch is complete and prevents anyone accidentally using old branches.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Delete your branch”
notes.evidence: After you merge your pull request, delete your branch. This indicates that the work on the branch is complete and prevents you or others from accidentally using old branches.

notes.front: In GitHub flow, what does creating a branch give you?
notes.back: A space to work without affecting the default branch, and a chance for collaborators to review your work.
notes.explanation: These are the two things the docs say a branch gives you at this step.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Create a branch”
notes.evidence: By creating a branch, you create a space to work without affecting the default branch. Additionally, you give collaborators a chance to review your work.

notes.front: After merging, a teammate hesitates to delete the branch in case its pull request and commit history are lost. Is the worry justified?
notes.back: A: no; the pull request and commit history are not deleted.
notes.explanation: The docs say you can also restore a deleted branch or revert the pull request if needed.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Delete your branch”
notes.evidence: Don't worry about losing information. Your pull request and commit history will not be deleted. You can always restore your deleted branch or revert your pull request if needed.
notes.choices:
A) No: the pull request and commit history stay
B) Yes: deleting the branch erases its commits
C) Yes: the branch can never be restored
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the docs say commit history will not be deleted. C is wrong: you can always restore a deleted branch.

notes.front: Halfway through a change in GitHub flow, Sara wants early advice from colleagues before she finishes. What can she do?
notes.back: C: open her pull request and mark it as a draft.
notes.explanation: GitHub flow lets you mark a pull request as a draft when you want early feedback or advice before completing your changes.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Create a pull request”
notes.evidence: If you want early feedback or advice before you complete your changes, you can mark your pull request as a draft.
notes.choices:
A) Delete the branch and start again
B) Merge the unfinished work so people can see it
C) Open a pull request marked as a draft
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: merging comes only after approval, and would put unfinished work on the default branch. A is wrong: deleting the branch is the last step, after merging.

notes.front: In GitHub comment fields and .md files, what are two of the text styles you can use for emphasis?
notes.back: Two of: bold, italic, strikethrough (subscript and superscript also work).
notes.explanation: The docs list five emphasis styles for comment fields and .md files.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Styling text”
notes.evidence: You can indicate emphasis with bold, italic, strikethrough, subscript, or superscript text in comment fields and `.md` files.

notes.front: In GitHub Markdown, how do you call out code or a command within a sentence?
notes.back: Wrap it in single backticks.
notes.explanation: Text within the backticks is not formatted.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Quoting code”
notes.evidence: You can call out code or a command within a sentence with single backticks. The text within the backticks will not be formatted.

notes.front: In GitHub Markdown, how do you format code or text into its own distinct block?
notes.back: Use triple backticks.
notes.explanation: Single backticks are for code within a sentence; triple backticks make a separate block.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Quoting code”
notes.evidence: To format code or text into its own distinct block, use triple backticks.

notes.front: In an issue comment, Ravi wants to paste a ten-line terminal session so it shows as its own block, unformatted. What should he use?
notes.back: C: triple backticks around the lines.
notes.explanation: Triple backticks format code or text into its own distinct block.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Quoting code”
notes.evidence: To format code or text into its own distinct block, use triple backticks.
notes.choices:
A) A > at the start of each line
B) Single backticks around each line
C) Triple backticks around the lines
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: single backticks call out code within a sentence, not a block. A is wrong: > quotes text; it does not make a code block.

notes.front: In GitHub Markdown, how do you create an inline link?
notes.back: Wrap the link text in square brackets [ ], then the web address in parentheses ( ).
notes.explanation: The docs give this as the syntax for inline links.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Links”
notes.evidence: You can create an inline link by wrapping link text in brackets `[ ]`, and then wrapping the URL in parentheses `( )`.

notes.front: Ana has written a task list in an issue. She has just finished the second item. How does she show it as done in Markdown?
notes.back: C: change its [ ] to [x].
notes.explanation: In a task list, [x] marks a task as complete.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Task lists”
notes.evidence: To mark a task as complete, use `[x]`.
notes.choices:
A) Put ~~ around the item
B) Delete the item
C) Change its [ ] to [x]
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: deleting removes the task rather than marking it complete. A is wrong: ~~ is strikethrough styling, not task-list syntax.

notes.front: When is a person notified about an @mention in a repository?
notes.back: Only if they have read access to the repository and, for an organization-owned repository, are an organization member.
notes.explanation: The docs set both conditions in a note on mentions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Mentioning people and teams”
notes.evidence: A person will only be notified about a mention if the person has read access to the repository and, if the repository is owned by an organization, the person is a member of the organization.

notes.front: Joe wants the team that looks after the docs to notice his question in a comment. What does he type?
notes.back: B: @ followed by the team's name.
notes.explanation: Typing @ plus a username or team name triggers a notification and brings their attention to the conversation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Mentioning people and teams”
notes.evidence: This will trigger a notification and bring their attention to the conversation.
notes.choices:
A) # followed by the team's name
B) @ followed by the team's name
C) The team's name in bold
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: # brings up suggested issues and pull requests, not people. C is wrong: bold text only changes styling and notifies no one.

notes.front: In a GitHub comment, what happens when you type #?
notes.back: A list of suggested issues and pull requests in the repository appears.
notes.explanation: You then type the number or title to filter the list and press tab or enter to complete the highlighted result.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Referencing issues and pull requests”
notes.evidence: Type the issue or pull request number or title to filter the list, and then press either tab or enter to complete the highlighted result.

notes.front: Writing a comment, Lucy wants to link to an issue whose title she remembers but whose number she does not. What can she do?
notes.back: C: type #, then part of the title, and pick the suggestion.
notes.explanation: After typing #, you can type an issue's number or title to filter the suggestions, then complete it with tab or enter.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Referencing issues and pull requests”
notes.evidence: Type the issue or pull request number or title to filter the list, and then press either tab or enter to complete the highlighted result.
notes.choices:
A) She must find the number first
B) Type @ and the title
C) Type # and part of the title, then pick the suggestion
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: @ mentions people and teams. A is wrong: the list can be filtered by title as well as number.

notes.front: Which GitHub alert type is for useful information that users should know, even when skimming content?
notes.back: The Note alert.
notes.explanation: GitHub offers five alert types, each for a different level of significance.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Alerts”
notes.evidence: Useful information that users should know, even when skimming content.

notes.front: Which GitHub alert type is for helpful advice for doing things better or more easily?
notes.back: The Tip alert.
notes.explanation: GitHub offers five alert types, each for a different level of significance.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Alerts”
notes.evidence: Helpful advice for doing things better or more easily.

notes.front: Which GitHub alert type is for key information users need to know to achieve their goal?
notes.back: The Important alert.
notes.explanation: GitHub offers five alert types, each for a different level of significance.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Alerts”
notes.evidence: Key information users need to know to achieve their goal.

notes.front: Which GitHub alert type is for urgent information that needs immediate user attention to avoid problems?
notes.back: The Warning alert.
notes.explanation: GitHub offers five alert types, each for a different level of significance.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Alerts”
notes.evidence: Urgent info that needs immediate user attention to avoid problems.

notes.front: Which GitHub alert type is for advice about risks or negative outcomes of certain actions?
notes.back: The Caution alert.
notes.explanation: GitHub offers five alert types, each for a different level of significance.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Basic writing and formatting syntax”, “Alerts”
notes.evidence: Advises about risks or negative outcomes of certain actions.

notes.front: Who may find GitHub Desktop easier than Git on the command line?
notes.back: People new to Git and GitHub.
notes.explanation: Its graphical user interface simplifies commands and helps you visualise changes.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Desktop”, “Benefits of GitHub Desktop”
notes.evidence: If you're new to Git and GitHub, you may find it easier to use GitHub Desktop than to use Git on the command line. GitHub Desktop has a graphical user interface that simplifies commands and helps you visualize changes.

notes.front: What is one less-common Git command that GitHub Desktop lets you use without memorising syntax?
notes.back: Choosing which changed lines to include in a commit (or adding a co-author to a commit).
notes.explanation: Its visual interface makes such commands easy to reach.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Desktop”, “Benefits of GitHub Desktop”
notes.evidence: Because GitHub Desktop has a visual interface, you can easily access less-common Git commands, such as choosing which changed lines to include in a commit or adding a co-author to a commit, without needing to memorize or look up syntax.

notes.front: A new analyst, unfamiliar with Git, needs to commit changes to a team repository on her laptop and wants to see what changed before committing. Which tool suits her best?
notes.back: B: GitHub Desktop.
notes.explanation: GitHub Desktop's graphical interface simplifies commands and helps you visualise changes, which the docs say may suit people new to Git.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Desktop”, “Benefits of GitHub Desktop”
notes.evidence: If you're new to Git and GitHub, you may find it easier to use GitHub Desktop than to use Git on the command line. GitHub Desktop has a graphical user interface that simplifies commands and helps you visualize changes.
notes.choices:
A) GitHub Mobile
B) GitHub Desktop
C) Git on the command line
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: GitHub Mobile is for triage and collaboration on a phone, not committing from a laptop. C is wrong: it works, but the docs say newcomers may find GitHub Desktop easier.

notes.front: What are two things you can do with GitHub Mobile?
notes.back: Two of: manage and triage notifications; read, review and collaborate on issues and pull requests; edit files in pull requests (among others).
notes.explanation: The docs list these among the tasks GitHub Mobile supports.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Mobile”, “About GitHub Mobile”
notes.evidence: With GitHub Mobile you can: * Manage, triage, and clear notifications * Read, review, and collaborate on issues and pull requests * Edit files in pull requests

notes.front: A maintainer is away from her desk and gets a push notification that she was mentioned on a pull request. She wants to read it and reply straight away. What should she use?
notes.back: B: GitHub Mobile.
notes.explanation: GitHub Mobile lets you receive push notifications for mentions and read, review and collaborate on pull requests from anywhere.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub Mobile”, “About GitHub Mobile”
notes.evidence: Read, review, and collaborate on issues and pull requests * Edit files in pull requests * Search for, browse, and interact with users, repositories, and organizations * Receive a push notification when someone mentions your username
notes.choices:
A) GitHub Desktop
B) GitHub Mobile
C) Nothing: she must wait until she is at a computer
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: GitHub Desktop is a desktop application. C is wrong: GitHub Mobile exists for high-impact work quickly and from anywhere.
